lead: A block diagram draws a control system as boxes joined by arrows. Each box holds one transfer function. A circle with Σ adds or subtracts signals. Block diagram reduction replaces the whole network by one transfer function from input R(s) to output C(s). The rules are algebraic: series blocks multiply, parallel blocks add with sign, and a feedback loop becomes G/(1+GH). Engineers use this to get a single model before time-response or stability work. It also shows how a take-off point or summing point can be moved without changing the input-output relation.
prereq: You need: transfer functions from 1.3 and the feedback idea from 1.2.

blocks.text: Name every block by its transfer function. Let G1 and G2 be two transfer functions. Let R(s) be the input and C(s) the output. Some syllabi call these rules block diagram algebra.

blocks.where: G is the combined transfer function; G1 and G2 are in cascade with no branch between them.

blocks.text: Series rule: multiply blocks when no summing point or take-off point sits between them. Parallel rule: add or subtract paths that start at the same node and end at the same summing point.

blocks.where: G1 and G2 are parallel paths from the same input to the same summing point; use + for the same sign and − for opposite signs.

blocks.text: Canonical negative feedback has forward path G and feedback path H. The error is E = R − H C. The forward block gives C = G E. Eliminate E to get the closed-loop transfer function.

blocks.where: G is the forward-path transfer function, H is the feedback-path transfer function, and GH is the loop gain; this is for negative feedback. For positive feedback use 1 − GH.

blocks.text: The sign at Σ belongs to the rule. A minus feedback sign gives 1 + GH. A plus feedback sign gives 1 − GH. Ignoring this changes the denominator.

sections.h3: Moving a summing point or a take-off point

blocks.text: A summing point is the circle Σ. A take-off point is a dot where a signal branches without changing the main path. Use ahead for upstream, towards the input. Use behind for downstream, towards the output. In each rule below, G is the block that the summing point or take-off point is moved across.

items: Summing point moved ahead across G: insert 1/G in the branch that now crosses the block. Check: G(R ± X/G) = GR ± X.
Summing point moved behind across G: multiply each input that used to enter the sum by G. Check: G(R ± X) = GR ± GX.
Take-off point moved ahead across G: insert G in the take-off branch. The tapped signal stays GX.
Take-off point moved behind across G: insert 1/G in the take-off branch. The tapped signal stays X.
Start at the innermost loop. Replace series and parallel groups inside it first.
Eliminate each feedback loop with C/R = G/(1 + GH). Keep the minus sign for negative feedback.
Move a summing point or take-off point only when a branch blocks reduction. Add the compensating block as above.
Repeat until one block remains. Check the dc gain at s = 0 as a quick test.

figure.caption: Series G1 = 2/(s+1) and G2 = 3/(s+2) feed a unity negative-feedback loop; the minus sign is at the summing junction. The worked example reduces this diagram to one block.

spec.aria: A negative-feedback block diagram with G1 = 2/(s+1), G2 = 3/(s+2) in series, unity feedback, and output C(s).

examples.question: Reduce the negative-feedback block diagram with G1 = 2/(s+1), G2 = 3/(s+2) in series and H = 1. Find C(s)/R(s). Also find the dc gain at s = 0.
steps: G1 and G2 are in series with no branch between them. G1 G2 = [2/(s+1)][3/(s+2)] = 6/((s+1)(s+2)) = 6/(s²+3s+2).
The feedback path is H = 1 with a minus sign. Loop gain GH = G1 G2 H = 6/(s²+3s+2).
Use the negative-feedback rule C/R = G/(1+GH). The denominator is 1 + 6/(s²+3s+2) = (s²+3s+2+6)/(s²+3s+2) = (s²+3s+8)/(s²+3s+2).
Divide the forward path by that denominator: C/R = [6/(s²+3s+2)] / [(s²+3s+8)/(s²+3s+2)] = 6/(s²+3s+8).
examples.answer: The closed-loop transfer function is C(s)/R(s) = 6/(s²+3s+8), and its dc gain is 0.75 (unitless).
examples.check:
num = 2 * 3
den_s = 1 + 2
den_c = 1 * 2 + num
dc = num / den_c
print(num)
print(den_s)
print(den_c)
print(dc)

traps: Dropping the minus sign at the summing junction. Negative feedback gives 1+GH, not 1−GH; positive feedback gives 1−GH.

Moving a take-off point without the compensating factor. A branch taken before G must get 1/G if moved after G (the tapped signal is GX there, so divide by G to keep X); a branch taken after G must get G if moved before G (the tapped signal is X there, so multiply by G to keep GX).
Adding parallel blocks without checking signs. G1+G2 applies only when both paths reach the summing point with the same sign; otherwise use G1−G2.
Applying the feedback formula to a loop that still contains series or parallel paths. Reduce the forward path and feedback path to one block each before using G/(1+GH).
Treating a summing point as a take-off point. A summing point adds or subtracts signals; a take-off point copies a signal without change.

quiz.q: State the series rule for two blocks G1 and G2 with no branch between them.
quiz.a: The combined transfer function is G = G1G2, so C(s)/R(s) = G1G2.

quiz.q: Why does negative feedback use 1+GH in the denominator while positive feedback uses 1−GH?
quiz.a: For negative feedback E = R−HC and C = GE, so C(1+GH) = GR. For positive feedback E = R+HC, so C(1−GH) = GR.

quiz.q: G1 = 1/(s+1) and G2 = 4/(s+2) are in series, with H = 1 negative feedback. Find C/R.
A take-off point after block G is moved before G. What block must the new branch contain, and why?
quiz.a: Insert G. The original tapped signal is GX; before G the signal is X, so the branch must multiply by G to keep GX.

quiz.q: A summing point before G is moved after G. The original output is G(R−X). Write the new equation and the compensating block in the X branch.
quiz.a: New output = GR−GX. The X branch needs a compensating block G before the summing point; R passes through G.

quiz.q: What is loop gain, and where does it appear?
quiz.a: Loop gain is GH, the product of forward and feedback transfer functions. It appears in the denominator 1+GH for negative feedback.

quiz.q: Why should inner loops and parallel paths be reduced before applying the feedback formula to an outer loop?
quiz.a: The formula G/(1+GH) expects one forward block G and one feedback block H. Inner paths must first become single blocks, or the formula is applied to the wrong paths.

beyond: Not for the exam. Block diagram reduction is the hand method behind Simulink and Modelica block models; software does the algebra, but the user still sets signs and branch points. In model-based design, engineers reduce a plant and controller to one transfer function for tuning, then simulate the full diagram. Search for block diagram algebra, Simulink model reduction, and Mason gain formula; the graph method is in 1.9.
